Spectral Jacobi approximations for Boussinesq systems

Angel Duran Address: Applied Mathematics Department, University of Valladolid, 47011 Valladolid, Spain Email address: angeldm@uva.es
Abstract.

This paper is concerned with the numerical approximation of initial-boundary-value problems of a three-parameter family of Bona-Smith systems, derived as a model for the propagation of surface waves under a physical Boussinesq regime. The work proposed here is focused on the corresponding problem with Dirichlet boundary conditions and its approximation in space with spectral methods based on Jacobi polynomials, which are defined from the orthogonality with respect to some weighted L2L^{2} inner product. Well-posedness of the problem on the corresponding weighted Sobolev spaces is first analyzed and existence and uniqueness of solution, locally in time, are proved. Then the spectral Galerkin semidiscrete scheme and some detailed comments on its implementation are introduced. The existence of numerical solution and error estimates on those weighted Sobolev spaces are established. Finally, the choice of the time integrator to complete the full discretization takes care of different stability issues that may be relevant when approximating the semidiscrete system. Some numerical experiments illustrate the results.

Key words and phrases:
Boussinesq systems, spectral methods, error estimates
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
65M70 (primary), 76B15 (secondary)

1. Introduction

1.1. Boussinesq systems for surface wave propagation

The four parameter family of Boussinesq systems of water waves

ηt+ux+(η​u)x+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t\displaystyle\eta_{t}+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
(1.1) ut+ηx+u​ux+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t\displaystyle u_{t}+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,

was introduced in [10, 11] as a 1D approximation of the Euler equations for the two-way propagation of an irrotational, free surface flow of an incompressible inviscid fluid in a uniform horizontal channel, [32], and the approximation is valid for long, small-amplitude waves, in the sense that

ϵ=ah<<1,λh>>1,S=a​λ2h2∼1,\epsilon=\frac{a}{h}<<1,\frac{\lambda}{h}>>1,\;S=\frac{a\lambda^{2}}{h^{2}}\sim 1,

where aa and λ\lambda denote, respectively, the amplitude and wavelength of the surface wave and hh is the depth of the channel. In (1.1), xx and tt are proportional to the position along the channel and time, respectively, while the real-valued functions η=η⁡(x,t),u=u⁡(x,t)\eta=\eta(x,t),u=u(x,t) represent, respectively, the free surface elevation at (x,t)(x,t) with respect to an equlibrium and the horizontal velocity of the fluid at a height y=−1+θ⁡(1+η⁡(x,t))y=-1+\theta(1+\eta(x,t)), for some θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] (with the bottom of the channel at θ=0\theta=0 and the free surface at θ=1\theta=1. In dimensionless variables, h=−1h=-1 is fixed.) The parameters a,b,c,da,b,c,d are given by

a=12​(θ2−13)​ν,b=12​(θ2−13)​(1−ν),\displaystyle a=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2}-\frac{1}{3})\nu,\;b=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2}-\frac{1}{3})(1-\nu),
(1.2) c=12​(1−θ2)​μ,d=12​(1−θ2)​(1−μ),\displaystyle c=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})\mu,\;d=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})(1-\mu),

where ν\nu and μ\mu are real constants. See [19] for a review on the systems (1.1).

The present paper is focused on the so-called Bona-Smith family, [12], of the form (1.1) with ν=0\nu=0 and b=db=d. This leads to

(1.3) a=0,b=d=3​θ2−16,c=2−3​θ23,\displaystyle a=0,b=d=\frac{3\theta^{2}-1}{6},c=\frac{2-3\theta^{2}}{3},

with 2/3≤θ2≤12/3\leq\theta^{2}\leq 1, because the system is linearly ill-posed if θ2<2/3\theta^{2}<2/3. (Note also that b=d>0,c≤0b=d>0,c\leq 0.) Limiting cases are θ2=2/3\theta^{2}=2/3 (a=c=0,b=d=1/6a=c=0,b=d=1/6 or BBM-BBM system) and θ1=1\theta^{1}=1 (a=0,b=d=1/3,a=−1/3a=0,b=d=1/3,a=-1/3). See [12, 11] for well-posedness results of the corresponding initial-value problem (ivp). One topic of research on (1.1) concerns the dynamics of its solitary wave solutions, [18]. The study is usually made via the numerical approximation to the corresponding periodic ivp of (1.1). However, some other phenomena which can be modelled with (1.1) consider the system on a bounded interval (a,b)(a,b) and with other types of boundary conditions for uu and η\eta at x=a,bx=a,b for t>0t>0. More specifically, here we will focus on Dirichlet boundary conditions for η\eta and uu.

The present work is greatly indebted to mainly two papers by Antonopoulos et al., [3, 4] and one by Bjørkavag et al., [8]. In [3], the authors analyze the well-posedness of several ibvp for the Bona-Smith systems on bounded spatial intervals [−L,L],L>0[-L,L],L>0. For the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, the main result is the existence and uniqueness of solution, locally in time, on suitable Sobolev spaces and on spaces of continuously differentiable functions of certain order. Before that, Bona and Chen, [9], proved a result of local well-posedness for the initial-boundary-value problem ( ibvp) with Dirichlet boundary conditions of the BBM-BBM system. On the other hand, [4] is concerned with the numerical approximation to the ibvp for the Bona-Smith systems analyzed in [3].The numerical approximation is based on the standard Galerkin-finite element method with piecewise polynomial functions for the spatial discretization and a fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta scheme as time integrator. Error estimates for the semidiscrete approximation and convergence of the full discretization are proved. The accuracy of the scheme is used to investigate computationally the interaction between solitary wave solutions and the solitary waves with the boundaries. Other error estimates, in the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, are obtained in [37] for the case θ2=1\theta^{2}=1 and the semidiscrete approximation with a nonstandard Galerkin finite element method; in [9] for the BBM-BBM system and a fully discrete finite difference method of fourth order in space and time; and in [15] for the BBM-BBM system when discretizing with a the Galerkin finite element method in space and a explicit multistep method in time.

The present paper proposes to approximate the Bona-Smith systems (1.1), (1.3) with Dirichlet boundary conditions by using spectral methods based on Jacobi polynomials for the spatial discretization and time discretization with special stability properties. The semidiscretization in space is motivated by [8], where a particular family of Jacobi polynomials, the Legendre polynomials, was already considered for approximating the ibvp of the BBM-BBM system, in order to study the onset of wave breaking connected with undular bores. The spectral approach based on Jacobi polynomials involves the use of suitable weighted inner products, [6]. This requires some previous analysis of the well-posedness of the problem on the corresponding weighted Sobolev spaces. On the other hand, the Bona-Smith system contains regularizing terms of BBM type, b​ηx​x​tb\eta_{xxt} and b​ux​x​tbu_{xxt}. As a consequence, the spectral semidiscrete system is not stiff when c=0c=0 and may have some stiff component when c<0c<0, due to the presence of the term c​ηx​x​xc\eta_{xxx}. This should have influence in the error estimate of the semidiscretization and in the choice of the time integrator. In addition, the last point may also be determined by the control of some stability issues of relevance, specially for long time simulations and when approximating problems from nonregular data. In the present paper we focused on the order of dispersion, [28], and the so-called strong stability preserving (SSP) property, [23, 24], related to the linear and nonlinear stability properties that prevent spurious oscillatory behaviour in the temporal discretization of the semidiscrete system.

1.2. Highlights and structure

The main goals of the project are:

  1. (1)

    The study of well-posedness of the corresponding ibvp with the proof of a result of existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solution, locally in time, on suitable weighted Sobolev spaces. The proof is based on similar arguments to those considered in [3] (in particular, the integral formulation of the problem) but adapted, in a nontrivial way, to weighted Sobolev spaces. This is treated in section 2.

  2. (2)

    Section 3 develops a convergence analysis of the semidiscrete Galerkin method based on spectral Jacobi polynomials, with the derivation of error estimates depending on the Jacobi weight and the regularity of the data. The lines of the proof involve a weak formulation of a related problem with homogeneous boundary conditions. In addition, several details on the implementation are provided. More specifically, the Galerkin-Numerical Integration (G-NI) formulation is described, and the relation with the spectral collocation approach is explained, [14].

  3. (3)

    In Section 4 the time integrators are introduced and their stability properties are described. The performance of the resulting full discretizations is checked, illustrating in particular the error estimates obtained in the analysis of the semidicretization in terms of the regularity of the solution.

2. Well-posedness

2.1. The initial-boundary-value problem

We will consider the following ibvp for the Bona-Smith system on Ω\Omega

ηt+ux+(η​u)x−b​ηx​x​t\displaystyle\eta_{t}+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}-b\eta_{xxt} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,

Remark 2.4.

As in [3], higher regularity of the solution can be derived from the hypothesis of more regular data. Using Remark 2.3, we can also extend the previous result in the following way: when hi,vi∈Cl​([0,T])h_{i},v_{i}\in C^{l}([0,T]) with l≥1l\geq 1, then there holds:

  • •

    If c=0c=0 and η0∈Hwm+2,u0∈Hwm+2,m≥1\eta_{0}\in H_{w}^{m+2},u_{0}\in H_{w}^{m+2},m\geq 1, then the solution of (2.7), (2.8) satisfies (η,u)∈CT0m+2×CT0m+2(\eta,u)\in C_{T_{0}}^{m+2}\times C_{T_{0}}^{m+2} with (ηtk,utk)∈CT0m+2×CT0m+2(\eta_{t}^{k},u_{t}^{k})\in C_{T_{0}}^{m+2}\times C_{T_{0}}^{m+2} for 1≤k≤l1\leq k\leq l.

3. Numerical approximation

In [4], the ibvp (2.1) is approximated using the standard Galerkin-finite element method for the spatial discretization and a fourth-order explicit RK scheme as time integrator. The present paper proposes a different numerical treatment, approximating the ibvp in space with a spectral Galerkin method based on Jacobi polynomials while the time integration is chosen according to the preservation of some stability issues that may improve the performance of the full discretization in long time simulations and with nonregular data.

3.3. Galerkin-Numerical Integration (G-NI) formulation

Described here is the representation used in practice of the semidiscrete Galerkin approximation and its relation with the spectral collocation approach. The representation is based on two main properties: the choice of a suitable basis of ℙN\mathbb{P}_{N} and the quadrature formulas for approximating the resulting integrals. Both are somehow related in the following sense. Some features of (2.1) (mainly the presence of nonlinear terms) typically require the use of a basis of ℙN\mathbb{P}_{N} of nodal type, which implies the choice of certain set of nodes {xj}j=0N\{x_{j}\}_{j=0}^{N} in [−1,1][-1,1] and the construction of interpolating polynomials ψj​(x),j=0,…,N\psi_{j}(x),j=0,\ldots,N such that

(3.21) ψj​(xk)=δj​k,j,k=0,…,N.\displaystyle\psi_{j}(x_{k})=\delta_{jk},\quad j,k=0,\ldots,N.

(Other choices, such as bases of modal tyoe, are not discarded, although they seem to give a better performance in the linear case, cf. [14, 36].) Then the selection of the xjx_{j} as the nodes of quadrature formulas used to approximate the integrals leads to a more convenient description of the semidiscrete system.

This general procedure is now described in more detail for the case at hand. Let w⁡(x)w(x) be a weight (1.4) for −1<μ<1-1<\mu<1 and let {Jn}n\{J_{n}\}_{n} be the family of the corresponding Jacobi polynomials associated to ww (that is, orthogonal to each other in Lw2L_{w}^{2}). Among several possibilities, the following Gauss-Lobatto-Jacobi formula is used as quadrature (the proof can be seen in e. g. [6]).

Theorem 3.2.

Let NN be a positive integer and {xj}j=0N\{x_{j}\}_{j=0}^{N} be given by x0=−1,xN=1x_{0}=-1,x_{N}=1 and {xj}j=1N−1\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N-1} as the zeros of JN′​(x)J_{N}^{\prime}(x) in (−1,1)(-1,1). Then there exists a unique set of N+1N+1 real numbers wj,j=0,…,Nw_{j},j=0,\ldots,N, such that for any p∈ℙ2​N−1​(−1,1)p\in\mathbb{P}_{2N-1}(-1,1) it holds that

(3.22) ∫−11p⁡(x)​w​(x)​𝑑x=∑j=0Np⁡(xj)​wj.\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}p(x)w(x)dx=\sum_{j=0}^{N}p(x_{j})w_{j}.

Note that (3.22) means that the quadrature rule, for integrals with weight ww, from the set {(xj,wj)}j=0N\{(x_{j},w_{j})\}_{j=0}^{N} is exact for polynomials of degree less than or equals 2​N−12N-1.

The nodal basis {ψj}j=0N\{\psi_{j}\}_{j=0}^{N} of ℙN\mathbb{P}_{N} based on the xjx_{j} and considered here is explicitly given by

(3.23) ψj(x)=C(N,μ)(1−x2)​JN′​(x)(xj−x)​JN​(xj),j=0,…,N,\displaystyle\psi_{j}(x)=C(N,\mu)\frac{(1-x^{2})J_{N}^{\prime}(x)}{(x_{j}-x)J_{N}(x_{j})},\quad j=0,\ldots,N,

where

C(N,μ)={1N⁡(N+2​μ+1)1≤j≤N−1μ+1N⁡(N+2​μ+1)j=0,N.\displaystyle C(N,\mu)=\left\{\begin{matrix}\frac{1}{N(N+2\mu+1)}&1\leq j\leq N-1\\ \frac{\mu+1}{N(N+2\mu+1)}&j=0,N\end{matrix}.\right.

The property (3.21) for the family (3.23) follows from the differential equation satisfied by the Jacobi polynomial JNJ_{N}, [6]

(3.24) dd​x​((1−x2)​JN′​(x)​w​(x))+N⁡(N+2​μ+1)​w​(x)​JN​(x)=0.\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}\left((1-x^{2})J_{N}^{\prime}(x)w(x)\right)+N(N+2\mu+1)w(x)J_{N}(x)=0.

We now describe the G-NI formulation to discretize the original problem (2.1)-(2.3) with the spectral Galerkin method based on the JnJ_{n}. (Recall Remark 2.1 as for the problem on general intervals [a,b][a,b] and the previous change to [−1,1][-1,1].) We first represent the approximations ηN,uN\eta^{N},u^{N} in the nodal basis (3.23)

ηk(t)=ηN(xk,t),uk(t)=uN(xk,t),k=0,…,N,t≥0.\eta_{k}(t)=\eta^{N}(x_{k},t),\quad u_{k}(t)=u^{N}(x_{k},t),\quad k=0,\ldots,N,\quad t\geq 0.

Remark 3.2.

The G-NI formulation makes the Galerkin method be essentially equivalent to a collocation approach, in the sense mentioned in, e. g. [14], and for the spectral collocation scheme based on the Gauss-Lobatto-Jacobi nodes xj,j=0,…,Nx_{j},j=0,\ldots,N, associated to the weight ww. For the case of (2.1), the semidiscrete collocation approximation is defined as the mapping (ηN,uN):[0,T]→ℙN(\eta^{N},u^{N}):[0,T]\rightarrow\mathbb{P}_{N} such that

ηtN−b​ηx​x​tN+(IN​(ηN​uN))x+fN\displaystyle\eta_{t}^{N}-b\eta_{xxt}^{N}+(I_{N}(\eta^{N}u^{N}))_{x}+f^{N} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
(3.41) utN−b​ux​x​tN+12​(IN​((uN)2)x+gNCLOSE\displaystyle u_{t}^{N}-bu_{xxt}^{N}+\frac{1}{2}(I_{N}((u^{N})^{2})_{x}+g^{N} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,

at x=xj,j=1,…,N−1x=x_{j},j=1,\ldots,N-1 with

(3.42) ηN(0)|x=xj=η0(xj),uN(0)|x=xj=u0(xj),j=0,…,N,\displaystyle\eta^{N}(0)\Big|_{x=x_{j}}={\eta}_{0}(x_{j}),u^{N}(0)\Big|_{x=x_{j}}={u}_{0}(x_{j}),\;j=0,\ldots,N,

satisfying (2.2), (2.3), and where IN​vI_{N}v denotes the interpolating polynomial of vv on ℙN\mathbb{P}_{N} based on the Gauss-Lobatto-Jacobi nodes. The implementation and analysis of (3.41), (3.42) make use of the discrete inner product

(3.43) (ϕ,ψ)N,w=∑j=0Nϕ⁡(xj)​ψ​(xj)​wj,\displaystyle\left(\phi,\psi\right)_{N,w}=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\phi(x_{j})\psi(x_{j})w_{j},

for ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi continuous on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, with associated norm ‖ϕ‖N,w=(ϕ,ϕ)N,w1/2||\phi||_{N,w}=\left(\phi,\phi\right)_{N,w}^{1/2}, and where the weights wjw_{j} are given in theorem 3.2. Thus (3.41) can be formulated from the representation (3.25) and making the inner product (3.43) of each equation with the nodal functions ψi,i=1,…,N−1\psi_{i},i=1,\ldots,N-1. The equivalence with the G-NI approach is based on the identification of the approximations of the integrals with the corresponding inner products involving (3.43).

4. Full discretization and numerical experiments

In this section the full discretization of (2.1)-(2.3) is completed with a discussion on the choice of the temporal discretization and some numerical experiments to illustrate the performance of the fully discrete method.

4.1. Temporal discretization

The following family of singly diagonally implicit Runge-Kutta (SDIRK) methods of Butcher tableau

γγ01−γ1−2​γγ1212\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{c | cc}\gamma&\gamma&0\\[2.0pt] 1-\gamma&1-2\gamma&\gamma\\[2.0pt] \hline\cr\\[-9.0pt] &\frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{2}\end{array}

is proposed as time integrator of the semidiscrete system (3.37)-(3.40). For a system of ode’s of the general form

(4.6) u′​(t)=F​(u),\displaystyle u^{\prime}(t)=F(u),

the formulation of the methods is given by

u∗\displaystyle u^{*} =\displaystyle= un+γ​k​F​(u∗),\displaystyle u^{n}+\gamma kF(u^{*}),
u∗⁣∗\displaystyle u^{**} =\displaystyle= un+(1−2​γ)​k​F​(u∗)+γ​k​F​(u∗⁣∗),\displaystyle u^{n}+(1-2\gamma)kF(u^{*})+\gamma kF(u^{**}),
(4.7) un+1\displaystyle u^{n+1} =\displaystyle= un+k2​(F⁡(u∗)+F⁡(u∗⁣∗)),\displaystyle u^{n}+\frac{k}{2}\left(F(u^{*})+F(u^{**})\right),

where unu^{n} denotes an approximation to the solution uu of (4.6) at t=tn=nk,n=0,1,…t=t_{n}=nk,n=0,1,\ldots, being kk the time step size. The method (4.7) is linearly implicit, requiring the iterative resolution of two intermediate systems (although the classical fixed-point algorithm typically works). The values γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 (implicit midpoint rule, order two) and γ=3+36\gamma=\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{6} (order three) will be considered below. Several properties justify our choice. First, we recall that the methods are A-stable (and therefore L-stable), cf. e. g. [27], as well as nondissipative. On the other hand, they are dispersive of order q=2q=2 and 33 respectively. The nature of this property (called phase error analysis or phase-lag analysis in the case of second-order equations) has been studied in many references in the literature, (cf. e. g. [22, 29] and references therein). A brief explanation of the theory and justification for its mention here follows. The origin is the study and design of efficient numerical integrators of ode’s (4.6) having oscillatory solutions. Such problems typically appear in spatial discretizations of pde’s of hyperbolic type or with some hyperbolic components. The goal is the analysis of the phase (or dispersion) errors and numerical dissipation of the free oscillations in the numerical solution, as well as the construction of schemes for their resolution. In order to measure these effects, the methods are studied when applied to linear systems with eigenvalues on the imaginary axis. Focused on Runge-Kutta (RK) schemes, the phase error analysis starts from the stability function R⁡(z)R(z) of the RK method which, as rational approximation to the exponential function, is called consistent of order pp when

R⁡(z)=ez+O⁡(zp+1).R(z)=e^{z}+O(z^{p+1}).

From this stability function RR, the dispersion or phase error is defined as, [28],

Φ⁡(y)=y−arg⁡(R⁡(i​y)),y∈ℝ,\Phi(y)=y-{\rm arg}(R(iy)),\quad y\in\mathbb{R},

where arg​z{\rm arg}z denotes an argument of z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}. The RK method is said to have dispersion order qq if

Φ⁡(y)=O⁡(yq+1),y→0.\Phi(y)=O(y^{q+1}),\quad y\rightarrow 0.

The fundamental relation between the order of consistency and the dispersion order is proved in [31]

Lemma 4.1.

Let pp be the order of consistency of a RK method with stability function RR. Then the dispersion order is q=pq=p if pp is even and q≥p+1q\geq p+1 if pp is odd.

This result is more specific in the case of DIRK methods.

Theorem 4.1.

Let p=m+1p=m+1 be the order of consistency of a DIRK method with stability function RR. Then the dispersion order is q=pq=p if mm is odd and q=p+1q=p+1 if mm is even.

In particular, for the SDIRK methods of tableau (4.1), the dispersion order is q=2q=2 when γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 and q=3q=3 when γ=3+36\gamma=\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{6}.

As mentioned in [28], for long time integrations of (4.6) with fixed stepsize, the dispersion is a relevant source of phase error causing the numerical approximation to become increasingly out of phase with the exact solution. Although the elements of the theory are defined and analyzed from linear oscillatory problems, it is expected to be of application in more general cases of (4.6) with solutions containing some oscillatory behaviour, in the sense that a method of high dispersion order will generate small dispersion errors of the corresponding oscillations that the numerical approximation may contain.

An additional, relevant feature of the two methods is concerned with the so-called strong stability preserving (SSP) property. This is briefly formulated as follows (see e. g. [26] for details). Let uF​Enu_{FE}^{n} be the approximation to some solution uu of (4.6) under study at t=tn=n​kt=t_{n}=nk, given by the forward Euler method and assume that, for some convex functional CC (typically some norm or seminorm) there exists kF​E>0k_{FE}>0 such that

(4.8) C⁡(uF​En+1)≤C⁡(uF​En),\displaystyle C(u_{FE}^{n+1})\leq C(u_{FE}^{n}),

for k≤kF​Ek\leq k_{FE}. From this assumption, and for a ss-stage Runge-Kutta (RK) method

yi\displaystyle y_{i} =\displaystyle= un+Δ​t​∑j=1sai​j​F​(yj), 1≤i≤s+1,\displaystyle u^{n}+\Delta t\sum_{j=1}^{s}a_{ij}F(y_{j}),\;1\leq i\leq s+1,
(4.9) un+1\displaystyle u^{n+1} =\displaystyle= ys+1,\displaystyle y_{s+1},

we define the associated SSP coefficient as the largest constant δ≥0\delta\geq 0 such that if k≤δ​kF​Ek\leq\delta k_{FE} then

(4.10) C⁡(yi)≤C⁡(un),1≤i≤s+1.\displaystyle C(y_{i})\leq C(u^{n}),\quad 1\leq i\leq s+1.

In particular, this implies the monotonicity preserving property C⁡(un+1)≤C⁡(un)C(u^{n+1})\leq C(u^{n}). If δ>0\delta>0, the method (4.9) is said to be strong stability preserving. The choice of the methods (4.1) with γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 and γ=(3+3)/6\gamma=(3+\sqrt{3})/{6} in this context is justified by the observation that they are optimal SSP methods within the SDIRK schemes with the same stages and order, in the sense that the value δ\delta in property (4.10) for k≤δ​kF​Ek\leq\delta k_{FE} is maximal, [21, 30].

4.2. Numerical experiments

In this section we show some numerical experiments to illustrate the accuracy and performance of the fully discrete schemes analyzed in the present paper. For the reasons explained in section 3.3, the subfamily of Legendre polynomials will be used as the spectral approximation in space. The experiments will be focused on the convergence of the methods and their performance when approximating problems with nonregular data, for which the error estimates (3.15), (3.16) of Theorem 3.1 cannot be ensured.

It may be worth explaining first some details on the computations. Let M>1M>1 be an integer and f∈Hk​(Ω),k≥0f\in H^{k}(\Omega),k\geq 0. In the computations below we will make use of the quadrature rule (3.22) based on the M+1M+1 Gauss-Lobatto-Legendre nodes xjx_{j} and weights wj,j=0,…,Mw_{j},j=0,\ldots,M, in order to estimate the HkH^{k}norms of ff via

(4.11) ∫−11|fOPENl)​(x)|2​𝑑x≈∑j=0M|fOPENl)​(xj)|2​wj,\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}|f^{l)}(x)|^{2}dx\approx\sum_{j=0}^{M}|f^{l)}(x_{j})|^{2}w_{j},

where fOPENl)f^{l)} denotes the llth derivative of ff.

The specific application of (4.11) is made from the following representation of the numerical solution at some final time t=Tt=T. Let N>1N>1 be an integer. From (3.25) the time integration with (4.1) provides approximations ηkN,ukN\eta_{k}^{N},u_{k}^{N} to ηk​(T),uk​(T)\eta_{k}(T),u_{k}(T), respectively, for k=0,…,Nk=0,\ldots,N. Then we consider the polynomials

(4.12) η~N​(x)=∑k=0NηkN​ψk​(x),u~N​(x)=∑k=0NukN​ψk​(x),\displaystyle\widetilde{\eta}^{N}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\eta_{k}^{N}\psi_{k}(x),\quad\widetilde{u}^{N}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}u_{k}^{N}\psi_{k}(x),

as approximations to (3.25) at t=Tt=T. If the numerical solution (4.12) is compared with an exact solution (η,u)(\eta,u) at t=Tt=T, then the corresponding norms of the errors are computed via (4.11). For those problems of which the exact solution is not known, the order of convergence in the spatial discretization is estimated from the quotients

(4.13) EN=‖(η~N−η~2​N,u~N−u~2​N)‖‖(η~2​N−η~4​N,u~2​N−u~4​N)‖,\displaystyle E_{N}=\frac{||(\widetilde{\eta}^{N}-\widetilde{\eta}^{2N},\widetilde{u}^{N}-\widetilde{u}^{2N})||}{||(\widetilde{\eta}^{2N}-\widetilde{\eta}^{4N},\widetilde{u}^{2N}-\widetilde{u}^{4N})||},

The first examples are focused on the convergence of the methods. We consider, for θ2∈(7/9,1)\theta^{2}\in(7/9,1), the solitary wave solution of the Bona-Smith family of the form, [17]

(4.14) ηs​(x,t)=η0​sech2​(λ⁡(x−cs​t−x0)),us​(x,t)=B​ηs​(x,t),\displaystyle\eta_{s}(x,t)=\eta_{0}{\rm sech}^{2}(\lambda(x-c_{s}t-x_{0})),\quad u_{s}(x,t)=B\eta_{s}(x,t),

with

η0=92​θ2−7/91−θ2,cs=4​(θ2−2/3)2​(1−θ2)​(θ2−1/3),\displaystyle\eta_{0}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\theta^{2}-7/9}{1-\theta^{2}},\quad c_{s}=\frac{4(\theta^{2}-2/3)}{\sqrt{2(1-\theta^{2})(\theta^{2}-1/3)}},

A second group of experiments illustrates the performance of the schemes with nonregular data. Recall that the error estimates (3.15), (3.16) depend on the regularity of the solution of (2.1) to be approximated. In this sense, for the nonsmooth case, some reduction of order of convergence and the generation of spurious oscillations in the numerical approximation are expected. All the experiments below are performed to approximate (2.1) in Ω=[−1,1]\Omega=[-1,1] with homogeneous boundary conditions, usng the third-order scheme (4.1) for γ=(3+3)/6\gamma=(3+\sqrt{3})/6 and k=0.1​hk=0.1h.

We first study the cases θ2=2/3\theta^{2}=2/3 (BBM-BBM system) and θ2=9/11\theta^{2}=9/11, with initial conditions

(4.19) η0(x)={1+2​x+x2−1≤x≤01+2​x−3​x20≤x≤1,u(x,0)=η0(x).\displaystyle\eta_{0}(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix}1+2x+x^{2}&-1\leq x\leq 0\\ 1+2x-3x^{2}&0\leq x\leq 1\end{matrix}\right.,\quad u(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x).

Note that the second derivative of η0\eta_{0} has a discontinuity at x=0x=0 and the presence of the term c​ηx​x​xc\eta_{xxx} should affect the regularity of the solution. The corresponding approximate solutions at T=1T=1 are shown in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.

We compute (4.13) at final time T=1T=1, using the H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1} norm when θ2=2/3\theta^{2}=2/3 and the H1×L2H^{1}\times L^{2} norm when θ2=9/11\theta^{2}=9/11. The results, shown in Table 5, suggest in both cases some reduction of the order of spatial convergence (recall that the example is out of the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1) and a spatial error of O(N−3/2)O(N^{-3/2}).

In the last experiments we approximate the BBM-BBM system with initial conditions

(4.20) η0​(x)=1−|x|,u0​(x)=0,x∈Ω.\displaystyle\eta_{0}(x)=1-|x|,\quad u_{0}(x)=0,\quad x\in\Omega.

The numerical solution at T=1T=1 is shown in Figure 4. Note that now the derivative of η−0\eta-{0} has a discontinuity at x=0x=0, but the evolution seems to regularize the η−\eta-profile, at least to allow calculating the H1H^{1}norm of the approximation.

Therefore, the values of (4.13) can be computed in the L2×L2L^{2}\times L^{2} and H1×H1H^{1}\times H^{1} norms. The results are shown in Table 6, and suggest an error in space of O(N−3/2)O(N^{-3/2}) in the first case and of O(N−1/2)O(N^{-1/2}) in the second.
